chapter.name: Circles
chapter.blurb: A pulley rope, a bicycle wheel touching the road, and a circular wire rotating about a point on it all motivate the chapter's central object: the tangent, a line that touches a circle at exactly one point and is really a secant whose two crossing points have merged into one. From there the chapter proves the tangent is always perpendicular to the radius at that point (Theorem 10.1), works out how many tangents a point can have depending on whether it sits inside, on, or outside the circle, and proves that the two tangents from any external point are always equal in length (Theorem 10.2). These two theorems combine to chase angles between a pair of tangents and the centre, compute tangent lengths using Pythagoras and similar triangles, and, their richest application, prove side and angle relations for triangles and quadrilaterals that circumscribe a circle.

scope_in.item: Recognise the three possible positions of a line with respect to a circle in a plane: a non-intersecting line (no common point), a secant (two common points), and a tangent (exactly one common point)
Understand a tangent as the limiting case of a secant, obtained when the secant's two points of intersection with the circle move together and coincide into a single point of contact
Know, from Activities 1 and 2, that there is one and only one tangent to a circle at each point on the circle, and that at most two tangents to a circle can be drawn parallel to a given secant

State and apply Theorem 10.1 (the tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact), including its proof that the radius is the shortest of all distances from the centre to any point of the tangent line

Use the corollaries of Theorem 10.1: only one tangent can be drawn at a given point of a circle, and the line containing the radius through the point of contact is also called the normal to the circle at that point

Determine the number of tangents that can be drawn to a circle from a point according to its position: none from a point inside, exactly one from a point on the circle, exactly two from a point outside (Activity 3, Cases 1-3)

Define the length of the tangent from an external point as the distance from that point to the point of contact, and compute it from the radius r and the distance d of the point from the centre using (tangent length) = sqrt(d^2 - r^2)

State and prove Theorem 10.2 (the lengths of the two tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal), by RHS congruence of the two right triangles formed with the centre, and by the alternative Pythagoras-based proof given in the Remarks
Use the corollary that the line joining an external point to the centre bisects the angle between the two tangents drawn from that point

Apply Theorem 10.1 together with the fact that a perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord to prove that a chord of a larger circle which touches a smaller concentric circle is bisected at the point of contact, and to find the length of such a chord given the two radii

Use the two right angles at the points of contact together with the angle sum of the quadrilateral formed by a pair of tangents and their radii to prove that the angle between the two tangents from an external point is supplementary to the angle subtended by their chord of contact at the centre, and that this angle equals twice the base angle of the isosceles triangle formed by the two tangents and the chord of contact

Combine equal tangent lengths, the perpendicular bisector of the chord of contact, and similar right triangles to find the length of a tangent from the point where two tangents to a circle meet, given the chord of contact's length and the circle's radius

Apply the equality of the two tangent segments from each vertex of a triangle or quadrilateral that circumscribes a circle (touches every side) to prove that the sums of opposite sides of a circumscribing quadrilateral are equal (AB + CD = AD + BC), and to find unknown sides of a circumscribing triangle from known tangent segments and the incircle's radius
Prove that a parallelogram circumscribing a circle must be a rhombus, and that the opposite sides of a quadrilateral circumscribing a circle subtend supplementary angles at the centre

scope_out.item: Finding the area of a sector or segment of a circle, or the length of an arc
scope_out.reason: These are the subject of the very next chapter, 11 Areas Related to Circles (p. 154), which the book's own Contents page places immediately after Circles; nothing in jemh110's 10 pages (144-153) computes an area or an arc length.

scope_out.item: Chord theorems carried over from Class IX (equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre, angles subtended by an arc, cyclic quadrilateral angle properties)
scope_out.reason: The chapter's own opening line says 'You have studied in Class IX that a circle is a collection of all points...' and treats such facts as already known; the one Class-IX fact it does reuse, a perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord, is applied (Example 1, Ex 10.2 Q7) but never re-derived or taught here as new content.

scope_out.item: Compass-and-straightedge construction of a tangent to a circle from an external point
scope_out.reason: This rationalised (Reprint 2026-27) edition has no separate Constructions chapter; jemh110 ends at page 153 with only the chapter's own Summary, and chapter 11 (p. 154) moves straight to sector and segment areas -- no construction steps appear anywhere in these 10 pages.

scope_out.item: Tangents common to two non-concentric circles (direct or transverse common tangents, or a tangent-length formula between two separate circles)
scope_out.reason: Every two-circle scenario in this chapter (Example 1, Ex 10.2 Q7) uses two CONCENTRIC circles sharing one centre O; a tangent common to two separate, non-concentric circles is never discussed.

scope_out.item: The circumference or area of a circle (2 x pi x r or pi x r^2)
scope_out.reason: No formula involving pi appears anywhere in this chapter; every numeric result comes from the Pythagoras theorem, triangle congruence or similarity, or the equal-tangent-length relation, never from a circle's own perimeter or area.

scope_out.item: Trigonometric ratios (sine, cosine, tangent of an angle) applied to the tangent-radius right triangle
scope_out.reason: Although the right triangle formed by a radius, a tangent length and the line to an external point (e.g. Theorem 10.2's proof, Ex 10.2 Q1) invites it, every worked example and exercise solution in this chapter uses the Pythagoras theorem and triangle similarity or congruence only, never a trigonometric ratio.

concepts.name: Tangent to a circle: meaning and existence
concepts.description: A line and a circle in a plane meet in 0 points (non-intersecting line), 2 points (secant) or exactly 1 point (tangent); a tangent is the limiting case of a secant when its two points of intersection coincide into a single point of contact; there is exactly one tangent to a circle at each of its points, and at most two tangents to a circle can be drawn parallel to a given secant.
concepts.idea: A tangent is what a secant becomes when its two crossing points merge into a single point of contact.
concepts.rule: For a line and a circle in a plane, exactly one of three cases holds: no common point (non-intersecting line), exactly two common points (secant), or exactly one common point (tangent, touching the circle at its point of contact). Rotating a line about a fixed point P of the circle (Activity 1) shows there is one and only one tangent at P. Sliding a family of lines parallel to a secant (Activity 2) shows at most two of them can be tangents.
concepts.example: Fig 10.1 shows the three cases for a line PQ and a circle. The rope on each side of a well's pulley (Fig 10.2, p.145) behaves like a tangent to the circle of the pulley. The wheel of a moving bicycle touches the ground along a tangent to the wheel's circle (Fig 10.4, p.146).

questions.a: As a secant is moved so that its two points of intersection with the circle move closer together, in the limit the two points merge into a single point of contact; a line touching the circle at just that one merged point is the tangent.
s: States that a secant's two intersection points can be brought closer together by moving the line
Explains that when the two points merge into one, the secant becomes a tangent at that point

questions.a: Only I and III

questions.q: Two students discuss circles. Aman says a line can meet a circle in three different points. Bindu disagrees and says a line can meet a circle in at most two points, and describes the three possible cases. Explain who is correct, and list the three cases Bindu should describe.
questions.a: Bindu is correct; a line can meet a circle in at most two points. The three cases are: no common point (a non-intersecting line), exactly two common points (a secant), and exactly one common point (a tangent).
s: States Bindu is correct and Aman is wrong

questions.q: A classmate claims: 'Since a tangent touches a circle at only one point, a tangent must be shorter than a secant of the same circle.' Evaluate this claim.
questions.a: The claim is false. A tangent and a secant are both lines, and their length is not fixed by how many points they share with the circle; 'touching at one point' describes the relationship between the line and the circle, not the line's length.
s: States the claim is false
Explains that the number of intersection points does not determine or limit the line's length

questions.q: Describe, in words, one circle together with one non-intersecting line, one secant and one tangent, all drawn with respect to that same circle, and state one distinguishing feature of each in terms of its number of common points with the circle.
questions.a: Sample construction: draw a circle with centre O. Draw a line well outside the circle, not touching it anywhere -- this is the non-intersecting line (0 common points). Draw a line crossing right through the circle so it enters and exits -- this is the secant (2 common points). Draw a line just grazing the edge of the circle at a single point -- this is the tangent (1 common point).
s: Correctly describes a non-intersecting line with 0 common points
Correctly describes a secant with 2 common points
Correctly describes a tangent with exactly 1 common point

concepts.name: Theorem 10.1: the tangent is perpendicular to the radius
concepts.description: Theorem 10.1 -- the tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact -- proved by showing the point of contact is the shortest of all distances from the centre to any point of the tangent line; its corollaries that only one tangent exists at a point of a circle, and that the radius through the point of contact is also called the normal to the circle at that point.
concepts.idea: Every other point of the tangent line lies farther from the centre than the point of contact does, and the shortest distance from a point to a line is always along the perpendicular.
concepts.rule: Theorem 10.1: if XY is a tangent to a circle with centre O at point P, then OP is perpendicular to XY. Proof idea: for any other point Q on XY, Q lies outside the circle, so OQ is greater than OP (the radius); since OP is shorter than the distance from O to every other point of XY, OP must be the perpendicular from O to XY. Corollary: there is one and only one tangent at any point of a circle. The line containing the radius through the point of contact is also called the normal to the circle at that point.
concepts.example: In Theorem 10.1's proof (p.146-147), a point Q on tangent XY other than P must lie outside the circle, so OQ is greater than OP. Exercise 10.1 Q3 uses this: a tangent PQ at a point P of a circle of radius 5 cm meets a line through the centre O at Q with OQ = 12 cm, and since angle OPQ = 90 degrees, PQ = sqrt(OQ^2 - OP^2) = sqrt(144 - 25) = sqrt(119) cm.

Concludes only one such perpendicular line is possible at P, so only one tangent exists there

questions.q: A tangent is drawn at point P to a circle of radius 9 cm with centre O. A point Q on this tangent is 41 cm from O. Find the length PQ.
questions.a: Since OP is perpendicular to the tangent at P (Theorem 10.1), triangle OPQ is right-angled at P. PQ = sqrt(OQ^2 - OP^2) = sqrt(41^2 - 9^2) = sqrt(1681 - 81) = sqrt(1600) = 40 cm.
s: Uses Theorem 10.1 to identify the right angle at P
Correctly computes PQ = 40 cm using Pythagoras

questions.q: Prove that the tangents drawn at the two ends of a diameter of a circle are parallel to each other.
questions.a: Let AB be a diameter of a circle with centre O, and let the tangents at A and B be l and m respectively. By Theorem 10.1, l is perpendicular to OA and m is perpendicular to OB. Since A, O, B are collinear (AB is a diameter), OA and OB lie along the same straight line, so l and m, both perpendicular to this one line, are parallel to each other.
s: States l perpendicular to OA and m perpendicular to OB by Theorem 10.1
Concludes l is parallel to m since OA and OB lie along the same line AB

questions.a: Let XY be a tangent to a circle with centre O at point P, and let PZ be the perpendicular to XY at P. By Theorem 10.1, OP is also perpendicular to XY at P. Since only one line can be drawn perpendicular to XY at the point P, the line PZ must be the same line as OP, so PZ passes through the centre O.
s: States OP is perpendicular to XY at P by Theorem 10.1
States only one perpendicular to XY can be drawn at the point P
Concludes the given perpendicular PZ must coincide with OP and so passes through O

questions.a: The student is not correct; l and m must be the same line. By Theorem 10.1, the tangent l at P is perpendicular to OP. Since m is also perpendicular to OP at the same point P, and only one line through P can be perpendicular to OP, l and m must coincide.

questions.a: This statement is incorrect. Theorem 10.1 specifically tells us the angle between the tangent and the radius through the point of contact: it states that this angle is always exactly 90 degrees, not merely that the two lines meet there.
s: States the claim is incorrect

If the needle-tip's line of contact is an exact tangent to the coin's circular edge at that point, then by Theorem 10.1 the radius of the coin drawn to that point of contact must be exactly perpendicular, 90 degrees, to the needle's line.
s: Describes a plausible real-life single-point contact with a circular object, distinct from the book's examples
States the tangent-radius angle would be 90 degrees by Theorem 10.1
Correctly identifies which radius (the one to the point of contact) this applies to

concepts.name: Number of tangents from a point, and the length of a tangent
concepts.description: A point's position relative to a circle determines how many tangents can be drawn to the circle through it: none from a point inside, exactly one from a point on the circle, exactly two from a point lying outside; for an external point P, the length of the tangent from P to the circle satisfies PT = sqrt(OP^2 - r^2), where O is the centre, r the radius, and angle OTP = 90 degrees at the point of contact T.
concepts.idea: Whether a point can touch the circle along a line depends only on whether it is inside, on, or outside the circle.
concepts.rule: Case 1: no tangent from a point inside a circle. Case 2: exactly one tangent from a point on the circle. Case 3: exactly two tangents from a point outside the circle. For an external point P, if O is the centre, r the radius, and T the point of contact of a tangent from P, then OT is perpendicular to PT (Theorem 10.1), so by Pythagoras OP^2 = OT^2 + PT^2 = r^2 + PT^2, giving the length of the tangent PT = sqrt(OP^2 - r^2).
concepts.example: Activity 3 (p.148) shows a point P inside a circle has no tangent through it, a point P on the circle has exactly one, and a point P outside has exactly two, T1 and T2 being the points of contact. Exercise 10.2 Q1: tangent length 24 cm from a point at distance 25 cm from the centre gives radius = sqrt(25^2 - 24^2) = sqrt(49) = 7 cm.

questions.a: The formula applies only to a point P outside the circle, where OP is greater than r, so that OP^2 - r^2 is positive; if OP were less than or equal to r, the point would be inside or on the circle, where a tangent either does not exist (inside) or has length 0 (on the circle), and OP^2 - r^2 would not give a valid positive tangent length.
s: States the formula applies only when P is outside the circle, i.e. OP > r
Explains that otherwise OP^2 - r^2 would not be a valid positive tangent length

concepts.name: Theorem 10.2: tangents from an external point are equal
concepts.description: Theorem 10.2 -- the two tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal in length -- proved by RHS congruence of the two right triangles formed with the centre (and, alternatively, directly by Pythagoras); the corollary that the line from the external point to the centre bisects the angle between the two tangents; applications to a chord of a larger circle touching a smaller concentric circle, and to computing a tangent length using the equal-tangent property together with the perpendicular bisector of the chord of contact.
concepts.idea: The two right triangles formed by the centre, the external point and each point of contact are mirror images of each other, so their corresponding sides, in particular the two tangents, must be equal.
concepts.rule: Theorem 10.2: if PQ and PR are two tangents drawn from an external point P to a circle with centre O, touching it at Q and R, then PQ = PR. Proof: triangles OQP and ORP are right-angled at Q and R (Theorem 10.1), have OQ = OR (radii) and OP common, so they are congruent by RHS, giving PQ = PR. Also OP bisects angle QPR, so the centre lies on the bisector of the angle between the two tangents. In two concentric circles, a chord of the larger circle that touches the smaller circle is bisected at the point of contact, since the radius to the point of contact is perpendicular to the chord, and a perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord.
concepts.example: Example 1 (p.149-150): two concentric circles with centre O; chord AB of the larger circle touches the smaller circle at P; AP = BP because OP (the radius of the smaller circle to the point of contact) is perpendicular to AB, and a perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord. Example 3 (p.150-151): chord PQ = 8 cm of a circle of radius 5 cm; tangents at P and Q meet at T; TP = 20/3 cm, found using the equal tangent lengths, the perpendicular bisector OT of PQ, and similar right triangles.

concepts.name: Angles between a pair of tangents and the centre
concepts.description: For two tangents drawn from an external point T to a circle with centre O, touching it at P and Q, the quadrilateral OPTQ has right angles at P and Q (Theorem 10.1), so angle PTQ and angle POQ are supplementary; also, in the isosceles triangle TPQ formed by the two equal tangents (Theorem 10.2) and the chord of contact PQ, angle PTQ = 2 x angle OPQ.
concepts.idea: Because each tangent meets its radius at a right angle, the quadrilateral formed by the centre, the two points of contact and the external point always has its two tangent-side angles fixed at 90 degrees each, which pins down how the other two angles must trade off against each other.
concepts.rule: For tangents TP and TQ from an external point T to a circle with centre O: angle OPT = angle OQT = 90 degrees (Theorem 10.1). Since the angles of quadrilateral OPTQ sum to 360 degrees, angle PTQ + angle POQ = 180 degrees (they are supplementary). Also, since TP = TQ (Theorem 10.2), triangle TPQ is isosceles, and angle PTQ = 2 x angle OPQ.
concepts.example: Example 2 (p.150): TP, TQ are tangents from external point T; proved angle PTQ = 2 x angle OPQ. Exercise 10.2 Q2 (p.151): if angle POQ = 110 degrees, then angle PTQ = 180 - 110 = 70 degrees. Exercise 10.2 Q3 (p.151): tangents PA, PB from P inclined at 80 degrees to each other, so angle POA = 50 degrees, since OP bisects angle APB (angle OPA = 40 degrees), and triangle OAP has a right angle at A, so angle POA = 180 - 90 - 40 = 50 degrees.

concepts.name: Circles inscribed in triangles and quadrilaterals
concepts.description: When a circle is inscribed in a quadrilateral or triangle (touches every side), the two tangent segments from each vertex to its two points of contact are equal (Theorem 10.2 applied vertex by vertex); this gives AB + CD = AD + BC for a quadrilateral ABCD circumscribing a circle, shows a parallelogram circumscribing a circle must be a rhombus, allows unknown sides of a circumscribing triangle to be found from known tangent segments and the incircle's radius, and shows opposite sides of a circumscribing quadrilateral subtend supplementary angles at the centre.
concepts.idea: Walking around a polygon that hugs a circle, each side is built from two tangent segments borrowed from its two end vertices, and those segments repeat in a pattern that forces the opposite side-sums to match.
concepts.rule: If a circle touches all four sides of quadrilateral ABCD at P, Q, R, S (on AB, BC, CD, DA respectively), then AP = AS, BP = BQ, CQ = CR, DR = DS (equal tangents from each vertex). Adding, AB + CD = (AP + PB) + (CR + RD) = (AS + BQ) + (CQ + DS) = (AS + DS) + (BQ + CQ) = AD + BC. If ABCD is also a parallelogram, opposite sides are equal, and combined with AB + CD = AD + BC this forces all four sides equal, making it a rhombus. For a triangle ABC with incircle touching BC at D, CA at E, AB at F: BD = BF and CD = CE, and the tangent length from A, AF = AE, can be found from the triangle's semi-perimeter and the incircle radius via area = radius x semi-perimeter.
concepts.example: Exercise 10.2 Q8 (p.152): quadrilateral ABCD circumscribes a circle, so AB + CD = AD + BC. Exercise 10.2 Q11: a parallelogram circumscribing a circle must be a rhombus. Exercise 10.2 Q12 (p.152): triangle ABC circumscribes a circle of radius 4 cm; BD = 8 cm, DC = 6 cm (D the point of contact on BC); solving via area = radius x semi-perimeter gives AB = 15 cm, AC = 13 cm. Exercise 10.2 Q13: opposite sides of a circumscribing quadrilateral subtend supplementary angles at the centre.

questions.q: A quadrilateral PQRS circumscribes a circle. If PQ = 12 cm, QR = 9 cm, RS = 8 cm, find SP.
questions.a: By the circumscribing-quadrilateral relation, PQ + RS = QR + SP, so 12 + 8 = 9 + SP, giving SP = 20 - 9 = 11 cm.
s: Correctly sets up PQ + RS = QR + SP
Solves to get SP = 11 cm

questions.q: Triangle ABC circumscribes a circle that touches BC at D, with BD = 6 cm and DC = 4 cm. If the tangent length from A is 5 cm, find the perimeter of triangle ABC.
questions.a: AB = AF + FB = 5 + 6 = 11 cm (using BF = BD = 6 cm). AC = AE + EC = 5 + 4 = 9 cm (using CE = CD = 4 cm). BC = BD + DC = 6 + 4 = 10 cm. Perimeter = 11 + 9 + 10 = 30 cm.
s: Correctly finds AB = 11 cm and AC = 9 cm using the equal tangent segments
Correctly finds BC = 10 cm and sums to get perimeter = 30 cm

questions.q: A triangle ABC circumscribes a circle of radius 4 cm. The circle touches BC at a point D, so that BD = 8 cm and DC = 6 cm. Find the lengths of sides AB and AC.
questions.a: Let the tangent length from A be t, so AB = t + 8 and AC = t + 6 (using BF = BD = 8 and CE = CD = 6). Then BC = 14 cm and the semi-perimeter s = ((t + 8) + 14 + (t + 6))/2 = t + 14. The area of the triangle equals radius x semi-perimeter = 4(t + 14). By Heron's formula, area = sqrt(s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)) = sqrt((t + 14)(t)(8)(6)) = sqrt(48t(t + 14)). Setting these equal and squaring: 16(t + 14)^2 = 48t(t + 14), so (t + 14) = 3t (dividing both sides by 16(t + 14)), giving 14 = 2t, so t = 7. Then AB = 7 + 8 = 15 cm and AC = 7 + 6 = 13 cm.
s: Sets up AB = t + 8, AC = t + 6, BC = 14 and the semi-perimeter s = t + 14
Correctly equates area = 4(t + 14) with the Heron's-formula expression and simplifies to t = 7
Correctly concludes AB = 15 cm and AC = 13 cm

questions.q: A quadrilateral ABCD circumscribes a circle. AB = 6 cm, BC = 7 cm, CD = 8 cm. A student computes AD using the equation AB + BC = CD + AD. Find what is wrong with the student's equation, write the correct equation, and use it to find AD.
questions.a: The student's equation is wrong: the correct relation pairs OPPOSITE sides, AB + CD = AD + BC, not the adjacent sides AB + BC and CD + AD. Using the correct equation: 6 + 8 = AD + 7, so AD = 14 - 7 = 7 cm.
s: Identifies that the student paired the wrong, adjacent rather than opposite, sides
States the correct equation AB + CD = AD + BC
Correctly solves to get AD = 7 cm

questions.q: A student argues: 'Since AB + CD = AD + BC for any quadrilateral that circumscribes a circle, this must also be true for every quadrilateral, whether or not it has an inscribed circle.' Evaluate this claim.
questions.a: The claim is false. The relation AB + CD = AD + BC depends on the equal tangent segments from each vertex, which only exist because a single circle touches all four sides; a general quadrilateral with no inscribed circle has no such tangent segments, so there is no reason for its opposite side-sums to be equal.
s: States the claim is false
Explains the relation depends on the equal-tangent-segment property, which requires an actual inscribed circle

questions.q: Construct, by choosing consistent side lengths, a quadrilateral ABCD that could circumscribe a circle, by picking values for AB, BC and CD and then finding the value AD must have. Then choose different values that could NOT belong to such a quadrilateral, and explain why not.
questions.a: Sample valid set: AB = 9 cm, BC = 5 cm, CD = 4 cm; then AD must satisfy AB + CD = AD + BC, so 9 + 4 = AD + 5, giving AD = 8 cm, a consistent circumscribing quadrilateral. Sample invalid set: AB = 9 cm, BC = 5 cm, CD = 4 cm, AD = 10 cm does NOT work, because 9 + 4 = 13 is not equal to 10 + 5 = 15, so no circle could touch all four sides of a quadrilateral with these four lengths.
s: Gives a valid set of AB, BC, CD and correctly solves for AD using AB + CD = AD + BC
Gives a second set of four lengths that fails the relation
Correctly explains why the second set cannot belong to a circumscribing quadrilateral
